cards.title: Inject custom Liquid sections into a Shopify theme
cards.summary: Mechanical click path for adding a custom Liquid section file to a Shopify theme so a bespoke product page can be built manually.
cards.use_when: You need to build a custom PDP section or page by hand in Shopify (no page builder), e.g. a branded product template for a new SKU.
steps: In Shopify admin go to Online Store, then Edit Code to open the theme code editor.
Open the Sections folder and choose Add a new section; name the file with a clear convention (in the source example: a product-specific name like [brand]_[product]_gg.liquid).
Paste your HTML/Liquid code into the new section file and Save.
To revise later, return to Edit Code, paste the new code over the old code, Save, then refresh the live page to confirm the change rendered.
Verify the current Shopify admin labels and menus yourself — theme editor layout changes over time.
caveats: Section code lives in the theme; theme updates or switching themes can drop or conflict with custom files.
Only edit code in a duplicated/published-safe theme if you cannot afford downtime.

cards.title: Assign a custom page template to a specific product
cards.summary: Click path for creating a product-specific template in the theme customizer and pointing one product at it so it renders a custom Liquid section.
cards.use_when: You want one hero/paid-traffic product to have a unique PDP layout while all other products keep the default template.
steps: Create the product first: Products, Add product, upload images, set price, and Save.
Go to Online Store, then Customize Theme and create a new template for the product (name it per product, e.g. hair_nectar_gg).
Inside that template, hide the default sections you do not want, then Add Section and select the custom Liquid file you created earlier.
Assign the specific product to the template so it populates the section.
Confirm the product page renders the custom layout and that the default template is untouched for other products.
Verify current Shopify template-assignment UI before relying on this path.
caveats: Template names are arbitrary but must match what you assign in the product; mismatches silently fall back to the default template.
Hiding default sections is not deletion — you can restore them if the layout breaks.

cards.title: Make a product actually buyable before launch
cards.summary: The minimum product-admin steps to stop a new product from showing sold out or unaddable-to-cart at launch.
cards.use_when: Immediately before driving paid traffic or launch content to a new product, to avoid wasting spend on an unbuyable PDP.
steps: Go to Products, Edit product on the SKU you are launching.
Set Available inventory (the source example used a large number like 10,000 for a launch SKU) and Save.
If drop shipping, confirm the fulfillment app or supplier actually holds that stock — Shopify inventory is only a number and does not create real stock.
After saving, add the product to cart yourself on the live store to confirm it is purchasable and the variant/price is correct.
caveats: Setting a large inventory number on a drop-ship SKU does not guarantee fulfillment; keep it aligned with real supplier stock.
If you later toggle inventory tracking, re-check the PDP still allows purchase.

cards.title: Reverse-engineer a validated product via a challenger angle
cards.summary: Score a candidate product across demand, ad momentum, store-level and competition signals, then only pursue it with a differentiating brand/content angle rather than a clone.
cards.use_when: Product selection: deciding whether to base a new store on a proven seller you found in ad libraries.
steps: Pick a product from a brand already scaling with active ads; treat sustained active-ad counts as the strongest ad-momentum indicator (source treats growing active ads as the key signal).
Score the opportunity across demand, ad momentum, store-level revenue/trust signals (e.g. Trustpilot), competition/concentration of top-spending ads, and Facebook/Meta ad-fit.
Check for a moat: if the winning tier is crowded and the moat is brand- and content-driven, a clone will lose — you must bring a sharp angle.
Check policies and ad-language compliance before committing, since category language can gate scaling.
If the score is high but the moat is brand-driven, plan for serious content and influencer support, not just a better product.
Treat the source's 7.95/10 'go with conditions' verdict as a heuristic example, not a benchmark threshold.
caveats: Scores combine one tool's ad-library data plus web research; without ad-library access expect materially less data (source cites roughly 55% of its data set).
Source opinion: a product can be validated yet still fail if you clone the incumbent instead of out-branding it.

cards.title: Capture competitor pages and ads as structured research inputs
cards.summary: Use screenshots of a proven competitor page as the seed input to product validation, branding, mockups and page-mirroring workflows.
cards.use_when: Starting any reverse-engineering workflow (validation, branding, product mockup, page clone) and needing a clean source image of the target brand page.
steps: Open the competitor's store page in the browser.
Use a full-page capture browser extension to screenshot the entire page, then download it.
Feed the screenshot into the research/branding tool as the reference brand you are modeling.
Note what is copied versus elevated: the source explicitly says it models what works but intends to improve pages, branding and voice rather than clone.
If visual references are needed, a page-image extraction extension lists every image on the page and lets you download them individually for use as inspiration inputs.
caveats: Downloading a competitor's imagery is for research/inspiration; do not ship their copyrighted assets as your own.
Screenshots are reference inputs, not validated product data — pair with ad-library and store-level signals.

cards.title: Build the brand kit before the store: intake, positioning and naming
cards.summary: Sequence for generating a usable brand system (strategy, voice, palette, logo, name) from a modeled competitor using an AI branding workflow.
cards.use_when: Building a new store's brand from scratch when you already have a validated product and a competitor to model.
steps: Run a branding intake with: specific product, business name, target market, price position, competitors, existing assets, and launch channel (the source used a US target market and a Shopify store).

Set brand-voice sliders (playful vs. serious, bold vs. soft), then answer the positioning prompts — source cites the 'dinner party test', '3-second feeling', and naming the territory/instinct questions.
Generate a brand strategy snapshot: colors, motif, product names.
Generate candidate names, then critique them against the actual customer; the source rejected names that felt disconnected and asked for names with 'hair' in them, which produced usable options.
Check domain availability and pick alternates (.co, .shop prefix, 'co' suffix) if the .com is taken.
Lock the name before generating assets so everything downstream stays consistent.
caveats: First-round AI names can miss the customer; plan to give corrective feedback rather than accepting the first list.
The source's chosen name and domain alternatives are examples, not recommendations for your category.

cards.title: Generate a brand board, then lock it for production consistency
cards.summary: Use a generative image tool to explore a brand board, then move it into a precise design tool to freeze logo and palette for suppliers and print.
cards.use_when: Preparing brand assets before sending a logo or packaging to a supplier or designer, or building landing-page visuals on-brand.
steps: Prompt a text-to-image tool to generate a brand board: logo, signature palette, pattern, headline treatment, element style and social vibe (the source used a poster-style brand board and preferred the most visual output over the most technical one).
Feed your accepted brand board back so the brand strategy can be finalized.
Generate logo concepts at a square (1:1) aspect ratio and pick one; the source generated four options and chose manually.
Move the chosen logo and palette into a precision design tool to recreate them exactly — generative tools approximate logos, which is unsafe for supplier files.
Export pixel-accurate PNGs of the logo in its variants and the exact color palette, so the mark never drifts across assets.
caveats: Generative image outputs are approximations — never send a generated logo to a supplier without recreating it precisely.
The source preferred one specific visual style/tool, which is a taste preference, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Write a brand reference guide for every downstream asset creator
cards.summary: Produce a short written brand description so mockups, product photography prompts and any hired creator can stay on-brand.
cards.use_when: Briefing product mockup generation, a photographer/videographer, or a designer and needing one consistent description of what the brand stands for.
steps: From your branding exercise, request a written description covering: what the brand is, what it stands for, its personality, and its unique identity.
Format it as a reference usable by a photographer, videographer or any asset creator.
Reuse the same guide as an input to product mockup and image generation so visuals stay consistent with the positioning.
Update the guide if the brand positioning shifts, so old asset prompts do not pull in stale mood.
caveats: The guide is only useful if it is actually pasted into every asset workflow; a file nobody opens changes nothing.
Keep it descriptive and specific — generic adjectives produce generic imagery.

cards.title: Draft the product mockup before contacting any supplier
cards.summary: Sequence for producing approved bottle and packaging mockups plus a clean pack shot from a competitor photo, logo, brand board and brand guide.
cards.use_when: Product sourcing and packaging prep: you need a visual target to send a supplier and to populate PDP imagery.
steps: Start with a competitor product photo so the tool understands the physical product you are making.
Add your logo, brand board, and written brand guide as inputs, then confirm the generated brand snapshot.
Name the first product with a consumer-friendly name (the source used a fun name instead of an ingredient name) and approve a bottle concept, e.g. a 'nectar window' label style.
Generate the base product image in the image tool at a print-friendly ratio (source used 3:4, 2K, medium) and generate multiple variations to choose from.
For image two, use your approved mockup plus your logo to generate lifestyle/setting shots; for image three, generate a clean pack shot.
Feed the approved images into a packaging brief to produce front/hero and back-panel packaging art, then send the product image and packaging spec together to the supplier.
caveats: Suppliers can improve on your spec — treat it as a direction, not a final print file.
Generated mockups are concepts; verify dimensions and label legal/ingredient copy before production.

cards.title: Create on-brand lifestyle imagery from competitor inspiration
cards.summary: Adapt competitor lifestyle shot compositions into your own branded images by pairing an inspiration image with your product reference and a written prompt.
cards.use_when: Building PDP, landing-page and ad creative imagery that looks on-brand without a photoshoot.
steps: Collect inspiration images from the competitor page (a page-image downloader extension speeds this up).
Pair each inspiration image (composition/lighting reference) with an image of your own product (identity reference).
Rewrite the scene for your formulation: the source swapped competitor props (e.g. white ice, oranges, lavender) for props matching its own ingredients (rosemary, cucumber, honey, avocado).
Generate at a usable resolution and iterate by swapping only the inspiration image while keeping the brand reference constant.
Use these images for the store, supplier presentations, influencer briefs and investor/pitch visuals.
caveats: Output quality tracks prompt quality — the source states images are only as good as the prompts.
Reusing a competitor's exact composition may risk looking derivative; change props, setting and brand cues.

cards.title: Sequence sourcing modes: dropship, then faster fulfillment, then private label
cards.summary: A staged sourcing recommendation: start dropshipping to test demand, upgrade fulfillment for speed, then move to private-label inventory as volume proves out.
cards.use_when: Choosing fulfillment/sourcing model for a new store built around a validated product, especially when launch capital is limited.
steps: Build the sourcing report for the product: supplier options by model, unit costs and margins, ETA and trust signals for each.
Launch on dropshipping first to take orders without inventory risk, using supplier product images for your store's product visuals.
Once orders are coming, move to a faster/domestic delivery option (source names ZenDrop/Spocket) to cut delivery time.
Once sales justify it, move into private labeling: order inventory, send your branding, have labels printed and the product prepared by the supplier.

If branded packaging is not yet affordable ($500–$1,000 stock example in the source), keep dropshipping and apply branding on the website and brand pages rather than the product — avoid showing branded product photos that mismatch the unbranded item the customer receives.
Do branding first anyway, as a target vision, even while shipping unbranded stock.
caveats: The source's model sequence (dropship → ZenDrop/Spocket → private label) is a recommendation, not a proven mandatory path.
A branded PDP with an unbranded shipped product creates a visible mismatch — the source explicitly warns against this; reconcile imagery with what actually ships.

cards.title: Mirror a proven competitor page into your brand as a starting structure
cards.summary: Use a page-mirroring tool to replicate a high-performing competitor page's section structure, then rebrand it to your palette and logo.
cards.use_when: Building a homepage, collection page or PDP for a new brand when you have a proven competitor page to model and no page-builder available.
steps: Open the proven competitor page and run the mirror tool to crawl and capture the page's full section structure.
Name the mirrored product/page and declare whether the page is transactional (customers buy on it) — checkout needs differ for buy-on-page vs. browse-only pages.

Watch the section-by-section build to confirm the tool captured the right structure; compare against the original section by section (hero media, description, video grid, reviews, FAQs, testimonials, footer).
Upload your logo and color palette and generate theme variants, then pick one that matches your brand.
Export/save your work (download the HTML) and re-upload to resume later — the source warns to always save before exiting.
caveats: Tool names, plans and buttons in the source are vendor-specific and may change — verify the current interface.
Mirroring produces a neutral structural template; you still need to rebrand copy and imagery or the result reads as a clone.

cards.title: Score and upgrade a mirrored page section-by-section
cards.summary: Audit a page against a scoring model, then add the missing sections it recommends rather than shipping the mirrored structure unchanged.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch page review: improving a PDP or homepage before spending on acquisition.
steps: Run the page score calculation so the tool evaluates existing sections and outputs a score plus specific missing-section recommendations.
Treat the score as a comparative heuristic, not an absolute benchmark: the source's mirrored page scored 55/100 and it added every recommended section.
Add recommended sections (the source suggested adding all of them), then manually reorder, hide, or add sections as needed for your offer.
Rewrite copy with AI as a separate pass rather than accepting mirrored copy.
Re-score after edits and compare before/after so the upgrade is measurable within the tool's model.
caveats: The 55/100 figure and 'add all sections' advice are the source's tool and opinion, not a published standard — judge whether each section fits your offer.
Adding sections can lengthen the page; do not add a block that has no real content behind it.

hint: baseline

Topics. store configuration.

Look for. The exact click path to inject custom Liquid code into a Shopify theme: Online Store -> Edit Code -> Sections -> Add a new Section -> Name the file (e.g., wle_hair_nectar_gg.liquid) -> Paste HTML/Liquid code -> Save.
